| Questions and approvals | A file inbox per project; `core_person_ask`, `core_action_approve` and MCP consent requests become cards in the app | Cross-handle round-trip tests, a full approval round trip through the engine |
| Runtime assets in pinned builds | Frozen and light pins, size estimates and project copies keep runtime files in `obj` folders. An `obj` directory beside a regular C#, F# or Visual Basic project file is still recognised as compiler output; ambiguous folders are retained. New pins record the direct-launch program relative to the copy so a newer helper cannot replace it; older pins retain discovery behavior | Synthetic filesystem tests cover both pin modes, model bytes, compiler-output controls and project duplication. A Linux tool-level regression starts temporary scripts through `project_pin_open`, with a newer `Build/obj/helper`, and verifies the originally selected program and its output; a missing recorded program is refused. No real pinned application was launched for this correction |
| Desktop app | Simple mode: sidebar with New project and the project history (kept across restarts); New project makes something, works on a project the person already has (Work on my project: its folder's files are the app, edited in place without a question, and the project takes the folder's name), or just looks inside an app or file, a website or a game's files; a Game files screen (a game's archives; pictures from Unreal paks, Unity .assets files and Unity bundles saved as PNG after the person confirms they may unpack the game; uncompressed textures and the block formats DXT1, DXT5 and BC4–BC7), make prompt with picture attachments (picked, dropped, or pasted with Ctrl+V, shown as picture tiles) and, for anything recreated, a Clean room / Deep choice (also in the title bar; in Clean room, Just look inside, Game files, opening a file and the workbench ask for Deep mode instead), project screen (steps with the time spent and the AI cost and tokens of every build, saved in the project's usage.json by the run (a coding agent's figure is shown as an estimate at API prices, not the bill), what the build is on now and its activity as it arrives (kept in `build-activity.log`), pinned builder checklist (its X folds it away between builds, kept in the project, `project_plan_fold`; a later run's checklist shows again; its steps scroll past a height set by dragging the divider above it, or with Up and Down, kept across restarts, #826), feed (each message and answer has a copy button, shown on hover or keyboard focus, #825), question and approval cards, a Continue card when a build was paused or stopped part-way (the app or computer closed; the project shows Interrupted) that carries on the builder's own session instead of starting over, and "It's done" beside Continue or Try again to keep the build as it is (`project_build_finish`), checks with screenshots and the requirements not met yet, the builder's open questions, preview, play, folder, follow-ups while it builds, which Claude Code takes at its next step; Up in the prompt box takes back the last note still waiting). Projects can start in a folder the person picks, whose files are either the app, edited in place (its stack read from those files unless the request names another, and, with nothing to recreate, judged by its own build and tests, whatever it's written in), or material to start from (asked, or the answer remembered in Settings), and are listed from any number of folders (`project_folders`, `project_list`, `rebuild --project-folder`). Make says which AI builds ("Built by": automatic, or any AI that can build, by name); a pick stays with the project and builds its later changes. With nothing to build with, Start offers the coding agents found on the computer. Settings → AI turns an AI off or removes it, and sets how hard the Claude API or Claude Code thinks (every Claude level, low to max; also `ai effort` in the CLI). Each Claude Code AI can keep its sign-in in a folder of its own (its `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so its own account; `ai folder` in the CLI, a folder on that computer over SSH), used for its runs, its sign-in check and its kept session, and Add another adds a second Claude Code for a second account. In the prompt box, Up at the very start and Down at the very end go through earlier prompts when no note is waiting. Questions about a build ("Just ask" under the prompt box, or a message starting with `/btw`, the first slash command; `rebuild_question_ask`) are answered in the conversation, where each folds away and is kept in the project, without a build or a round and changing nothing: Claude Code answers from a read-only copy of the builder's own session. Under each project's prompt box, "Builder's questions: Ask me / Decide yourself" chooses whether the builder's questions come to the person as cards or are decided by the builder, which says what it chose (`project_questions_set`; the default is in Settings and follows Auto mode until picked). Projects can be renamed, duplicated and deleted (right-click in the sidebar, or the project's page; a delete keeps the person's own files). A build can be pinned (Pin this build on its page, or `project_pin_*` from the CLI and MCP): a frozen copy in the project's pinned/ folder (the default) or a light one that shares dependencies and media with the project through hard links (each one's size shown first), opened from the sidebar's collapsible Pinned section (icons with a running dot when folded); a pin or Play runs once per folder unless another copy is asked for, and a start that quits at once says so with its last output. Typed drafts survive a restart. In a narrow window the sidebar folds to icons and the project's details move above its feed; messages float over the screen and errors stay until dismissed. Advanced mode: workbench with every panel wired to real tools, as a screen beside the projects (builds and their questions stay a click away). On macOS the menu bar has the app's actions (open, new project, settings, Simple / Advanced, Clean room / Deep, the command palette, help) with the usual shortcuts | UI unit and smoke tests (egui_kittest), offscreen snapshots of every screen |
| CLI | Every tool, `--deep` or `--clean-room` for one run (never saved), `rebuild` (including `--continue-in`, and `--resume` to carry on a stopped build), `mcp --inbox`, `ai`, `setup`, `doctor`, `report` | CLI integration tests |
| SQLite database files (`db_sqlite_show`) | A rowid alias column (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, including the table-constraint form) shows the rowid; `DESC`, non-`INTEGER` and composite keys keep their stored values | Hand-built fixtures; generated files compared with the official SQLite library |

### Builder retry policy

Builder failures carry a typed reason through `Conversation::last_failure`. Typed authentication,
billing, missing programs, unavailable tools, configuration and unknown protocol failures stop
for attention. Transport interruptions, rate limits and nonzero process exits without a typed
error get at most three retries; the decision no longer searches English error messages.
Structured provider waits win; the earlier numeric “retry in”
hint is only a delay fallback after a failure has already been classified as retryable. All waits
remain cancellable and bounded to fifteen minutes.
Local inbox and workspace write failures are not retried using a concurrent backend failure's
retry advice; the original local error is returned.
A missing saved session starts afresh only when a fresh request is available; otherwise the run
stops without retrying the unavailable session.

Claude Code's failed or unauthenticated `craft-anything` MCP server in its init event stops the
owned CLI process. Pending servers and failures in unrelated optional servers do not stop it.
Claude assistant error codes, HTTP status/provider errors and ACP authentication errors retain
their typed meanings. A later generic result does not erase a more specific error.

API retries continue the existing history without inserting the user's message again or replaying
completed tools. Stateless CLI retries receive the whole original request. OpenCode now uses
`run --format json`: its API error status and retry flag decide retryability while text, tools and
usage still reach the feed. Missing or invalid step costs keep the turn's cost unknown; explicit
zero remains a known cost. A CLI that fails with only a numeric exit also uses bounded retries;
its display error remains available if recovery fails. The process wrapper sends one final turn
event and becomes available for the next request.

Protocol fixtures, a loopback HTTP server, scripted API turns and executable CLI stand-ins cover
these paths, including cancellation and the retry cap. An executable that exits 1 without a
structured error resumes its saved session, while typed setup errors retain priority over the
same exit status. No live provider or paid-model run was performed. The separate source of #64's
41 attempts remains unverified.

### Bun stored-text encoding

Packed Bun members with encoding value 2 are labelled `utf16le`, matching their stored UTF-16LE
bytes. Reading or unpacking preserves those bytes. Synthetic graphs cover UTF-16LE (including a
surrogate pair), Latin1 and binary members across both supported module-record and offsets-block
sizes. A freshly compiled Bun program and the CLI/MCP transport were not run for this correction.

### Native tool-call stop reasons

Native OpenAI-compatible tool calls retain a reported output limit or refusal instead of
replacing it with a tool-use stop. The conversation can therefore reject those calls before
running a tool, including calls whose arguments happen to be valid JSON. A normal `stop`
with tool calls still works for servers that omit `tool_calls` as the finish reason.
Calls retained after a pause or another terminal stop get matching non-execution results,
so subsequent requests keep valid tool-call history. A pause continues the same turn;
terminal stops wait for the next user message.
Checked with streamed-call fixtures and HTTP/SSE stand-ins through the real conversation
and engine loop. Three history-pairing regressions fail without the follow-up and pass with
it. The affected crate's 223 tests and Clippy checks passed locally. The initial stop-reason
correction also passed [hosted CI](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/actions/runs/41587580930)
in PR #544. This correction concerns reported finish reasons; handling of a missing finish
reason is unchanged. No live provider or local-model build was run.

### OpenCode review follow-up

OpenCode variants now use the shared five-level `Effort` type while retaining exact catalogue
validation. Hub and headless tool selections share a strict disk-based save that preserves unrelated
settings changes and refuses damaged files or changed backends. Regression tests cover both entry
points. Rejected or cancelled model validation emits a terminal turn event so headless chat exits.

### Unreal setup

Unreal installations registered in `~/.config/Epic/UnrealEngine/Install.ini` are found on Linux.
A valid absolute `UE_ROOT` selects an installation explicitly; an invalid override falls back to
registered installations. The version comes from `Engine/Build/Build.version`, and C++ readiness
checks for the selected engine's bundled Clang, not an unrelated system compiler or another
installation's SDK. The Linux requirements summary (`Builder::needs` for Unreal) now describes
the bundled Clang toolchain. The guided installer now gives Linux-specific guidance: it names the
bundled Clang and points at the engine's `Engine/Build/BatchFiles/Linux/SetupToolchain.sh` (or `Setup.sh`
for a source build) when Clang is missing. On macOS, the status line and requirements summary now
name Xcode, matching the guided step. The guidance strings are unit-tested; no live Unreal
install or macOS run was performed for this copy change.

Checked with isolated registry and SDK fixtures and with a native Fedora install of Unreal
5.8.4. On Windows, Visual Studio C++ readiness also checks instances registered in
`%ProgramData%\Microsoft\VisualStudio\Packages\_Instances\*\state.json` and explicit developer
environment roots (`VSINSTALLDIR`, `VCINSTALLDIR`, `VCToolsInstallDir`), requiring `cl.exe`
under an MSVC toolset's `bin` tree rather than an empty `VC/Tools/MSVC` or version folder; checked with isolated
fixtures and on Windows 11 against Visual Studio Community 2026 (`18.9.2`, MSVC `14.51.36231`).
Readiness is a tool-presence check; a complete Unreal game build and SDK compatibility
validation have not been run for this change.

### Provider error messages

HTTP failures include the provider's message from `error.metadata.raw`, when it contains a
message, detail or string error. Object payloads, JSON-encoded strings and plain-text reasons
are supported, with the provider's name when supplied. A repeated outer message does not hide a
distinct nested detail. JSON-string wrappers are decoded to a bounded depth before reading message
fields; arbitrary, malformed or excessively wrapped structured metadata is not dumped. HTTP status
classification and remediation are retained, and displayed details are bounded by Unicode characters.
Checked with synthetic response bodies, repeated messages, encoded payloads with adjacent headers,
malformed metadata and Unicode length controls. The affected crate's 222 tests and all-target Clippy
checks passed locally for PR #542. No live API-key build or account-specific diagnosis was performed.

### Fixed during the audit

Web tools couldn't launch a browser on Windows/macOS (Chrome/Edge are off PATH) or be pointed at
a URL; the desktop app looked tools up by ids that didn't exist (website, phone, imports,
classes, modules, pseudo-C, disassembly, source and network panels were dead); evidence wasn't
reloaded from a project in a new process; report citations were unresolved; the CLI's
`--format` clashed with tools' own `format`; raw binaries couldn't be opened from the CLI;
function discovery claimed complete coverage when capped; .NET/Go binaries were called
"stripped"; Windows path separators and CRLF checkouts broke two tests; decompiler tail calls
and Win64 stack arguments. Added since: byte search, Rust binaries, Electron fuses, WASM
interface diff, packet captures, objdump, rizin commands, GDB sessions, then rizin debug sessions (`native_rizin_session_*`,
checked with Rizin 0.9.1 on Windows) and radio decoding with rtl_433 (`radio_recording_decode`,
`radio_decoders_list`, checked with rtl_433 25.12 on Windows) and Cutter sessions the person
shares with `=h& 9090` (`native_cutter_sessions_list`, `native_cutter_command_run`; tested
against a stand-in server, not yet a real Cutter). Every tool is listed in `docs/tools.md`.

### SquashFS extended directories

The filesystem reader recovers the same files and bytes from basic and extended directory inodes.
Synthetic images cover an extended root, a nested extended directory with a nonzero listing offset,
and both together; the results are compared with the existing basic-directory fixture. Compressed
metadata, directory indexes and a real firmware extraction were not newly checked for this fix.

### Keep-awake helper cleanup

Rebuilds release their keep-awake guard before emitting `Finished` and clearing the running flag.
The guard waits up to five seconds for the owned helper's supervised cleanup, logging a warning
if that deadline passes. Cleanup runs on the rebuild worker, with a bounded shutdown wait.

Checked on Linux with real subprocess stand-ins: dropping a guard closes the helper's listener,
a stand-in CLI can drop it and exit immediately without leaving the helper running, and an
already-finished helper releases promptly. The immediate-exit case fails with the earlier
asynchronous cleanup. The intermittent Windows report and Windows/macOS sleep inhibition have
not been rechecked for this change; Windows runtime validation remains on the roadmap.

The full workspace gates (`cargo xtask ci`) passed in [hosted CI for #541](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything/actions/runs/41584228995).

### Tool calls written as JSON

The text fallback accepts complete bare or fenced JSON calls with `name` and `arguments`
(`parameters` also accepted), including a `function` wrapper and JSON-encoded arguments.
Automatic recovery also handles these responses when native tool calling was offered. A call
must name a tool offered in that turn; ordinary JSON answers and JSON examples surrounded by
prose are left as text. Native calls are kept once; text-call recovery skips truncated or refused replies.
Complete backtick-fenced legacy ReAct steps remain supported when their body begins with an explicit
protocol marker. Both parsers use the same fence boundaries: at least three opening backticks and a
standalone closing line of at least that length, with no earlier matching closing fence. Shorter
backtick lines inside a longer fence remain content. Ordinary fenced code, malformed fences and non-call
JSON objects or examples containing protocol markers remain text; valid call arguments may contain those markers.
The parser regressions failed on the previous guards and passed with their corrections.
Fenced JSON calls also use these boundaries during automatic recovery and accept only an empty or `json` info string.
Checked with parser fixtures, HTTP/SSE stand-ins exercising real engine tool execution in both
protocols, and non-action, stop-reason and duplicate-call controls. No live local-model build
was run; other text-call formats remain unsupported.

### Linux graphics card choice

On Linux the desktop app draws on the GPU that drives the screen (#571), read from the connected
displays in `/sys/class/drm`: the built-in panel's GPU on a laptop, the only GPU with monitors on a
desktop, and the discrete GPU when monitors are on more than one GPU or nothing can be read.
`WGPU_ADAPTER_NAME` and `WGPU_POWER_PREF` still decide when set. `desktop.log` says which adapter
was chosen and why.

Checked live on one laptop (AMD Renoir iGPU driving the panel, NVIDIA RTX 3050, CachyOS, KDE
Plasma on Wayland): the window opens in 3 s on the AMD GPU instead of 18–25 s on NVIDIA, and the
desktop no longer lags; `WGPU_POWER_PREF=high`, `WGPU_ADAPTER_NAME=nvidia` and `DRI_PRIME=1` with
`WGPU_POWER_PREF=none` still draw on NVIDIA. Desktops with monitors on one or two GPUs and Intel
laptops are covered by unit tests on fake `/sys/class/drm` folders only.

## Known limits

- Locks: every mutex but the browser viewer's goes through `platform::sync`. A deadlock on one thread or across
  threads is broken when it forms, with an error and a report in `logs/`; a watchdog looks every 5 s; a holder
  that isn't a labelled job is reported after 2 minutes and waited on for 15 at most. Tools are labelled, so they
  may run as long as they need. Checked by unit tests of each case, not by a live deadlock in the desktop app.
  Waits on channels and `join` aren't watched; each child program has its own deadlines.
- A failed agent CLI run says what ran and what it printed, and writes a private log to `logs/` in the
  config folder (the newest 50 are kept; the person's message is left out; **Open log** in the app, `log:`
  in the CLI). Checked live against a GitHub ssh alias from the CLI; the button by a UI test, not by
  clicking it in the desktop app. API backends and MCP start-up don't write these logs yet.
- Live end-to-end runs (2026-10-18, Windows 10, headless CLI): a website clone reached Ready
  at 96% likeness in 1.5 min; a small desktop app rebuilt in Rust + egui reached Ready in 9 min (checked
  only by building); a game rebuild in Rust reached Build and was stopped before Check. The
  website case is an opt-in test: `CRAFT_E2E=1 cargo test -p craft-anything-cli --test live_rebuild`.
- Approvals differ by agent (roadmap R2.2): Claude Code asks our approval tool; OpenCode's builder
  runs with `--auto`; Hermes's `-z` turns its approvals off on every run, chats included, so a Hermes
  chat isn't limited to analysing and Clean room's approval rule doesn't reach it. Hermes is opt-in
  and hasn't been run live here.
- Maki (`maki -p`, or over ACP with `acp = true`) is offered when adding a coding agent and found by
  Detect. Over ACP it asks us before commands, our own tools and writes outside its working folder;
  writes inside that folder (a build's project folder, our own records included) and every read
  never ask, so the approval policy and Clean room's read rule don't reach those. Plain `maki -p`
  doesn't ask at all, so a Clean room build's reads aren't checked either; outside a build it runs
  with its writing tools, shell and code execution switched off, and Maki refuses anything else
  that would ask (an MCP server's tools, in subagents too) unless the person allowed it in Maki's
  own permissions. It hasn't been run as a `maki -p` builder here.
- Claude Code is fully wired as a builder; Codex works through its own flags (our tools are pre-approved for
  `codex exec` and every tool permitted by the current mode is listed from startup, see `docs/codex.md`)
  but doesn't resume. Codex 0.166.0 received the full Clean room inventory through a loopback model;
  no real-account build has been run;
  Copilot builds, model discovery and real-account session
  resume were confirmed by the person using the app. Other agent programs
  without an adapter get plain text in and out. API-key
  backends (Anthropic, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Gemini through a Google AI Studio key, local; Kimi K3.1 Pro through OpenRouter is offered by Detect; a backend chosen as the Extractor takes a Deep-mode game's own files out into `app/Original/` after the study) build with our own loop and the Build tools,
  trim and summarise long conversations and keep them in `transcript.json`; no live API build has
  been run yet.
- Website checks compare the start page and up to 12 linked pages at the configured widths; the
  start page's menus, pop-ups and tabs are opened on the build too and compared in the note (the
  first few only, never menus inside menus or hover-only ones). Apps and games are checked by
  building and by a screenshot compared with the person's pictures (and the original's window
  when runtime study is on; then the build is also started normally, and its window and
  labelled controls are compared with the original's); games (and apps decompiled in Deep mode)
  also keep `app/mechanics.json`, which is checked for being readable and sourced, and fails
  while a number found in the original isn't used in the code (estimates may stay out). Every
  game must also pass its own `--self-test` (the build plays its core loop with scripted input
  and reports whether the player moved, acted and the HUD was drawn), and a Deep-mode game that
  uses the original's files must have `app/CREDITS.md` and the private-use line in
  `app/README.md`. The self-test is the build's own report: Craft Anything doesn't yet watch the
  game play or measure the values itself.
- In Deep mode, app and game targets get a static study (triage, engine detection, file
  inventory, JS app graph, Ghidra when installed); in Clean room only the person's pictures and
  words. With runtime study on, the original is also started once for a
  picture of its window and its UI tree (Windows and macOS); it isn't driven or watched over time.
- Several projects build at once (`[build] parallel`, 2 by default; Settings → Builds); more wait
  their turn. Queued builds start on their own as places come free, from MCP too.
- Some flows exist only in the desktop app: the project feed, game-engine and Ghidra installs,
  and launching results (ROADMAP R1.6).
- Engine gaps from the audit: Frida session tools are partly simulated; imports outside the
  argument-count table show only the arguments set in the calling block. See tool-status.md.

## Next

See [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) for the ordered plan.

## Build progress across runs

When app files can be compared, a build stops after two consecutive completed builder turns leave them unchanged.
The versioned `inbox/build-progress.json` record keeps that count when the project is reopened or
Try again is pressed. File contents and executable permissions decide progress, so rewriting
identical bytes does not reset it. An actual app edit or a new nonempty request starts another
attempt, including notes queued during a turn or check and notes consumed by a builder hook.
Empty notes and plain Try again keep the saved count. Dependency/build caches,
git metadata and Craft's own records, including checks in a project edited in place, do not count.
Symlinks are recorded without following their targets. A successful check may still finish the
second unchanged turn, and a run waiting only for checks does not start the builder again.
Within a run, file digests are reused while size, modification time and executable bits match;
Unix file identity and change time also invalidate a cached read. The first scan reads content,
but unchanged imported assets are not read again before and after every turn. The metadata is
only a cache key: rewriting identical bytes still produces the same content fingerprint.
The cache is isolated by project root, drops deleted or retyped paths, and is discarded after
scan errors or cancellation. It is not persisted, and the version-1 fingerprint/schema is unchanged.
Sockets, pipes and devices contribute their names and types without opening their contents.
If a scan cannot finish because of limits, permissions or changing files, the feed says why the
unchanged-turn limit is skipped for that run. The saved fingerprint and count are cleared so a
later readable run starts a fresh comparison. Checks and the existing round limit still apply.
Cancellation still stops the run; completed builder replies are saved as awaiting checks before
the post-turn scan. Broken or newer progress records and record-write failures remain errors.

Scripted API turns and executable CLI stand-ins cover the stop, persistence, fresh requests and
check recovery. This change has not been verified with a paid model or a live provider. Copying a
whole project keeps its progress record; Duplicate creates a new attempt with a fresh conversation
and count, as it already does for usage.
An existing root-level file or directory named `build-progress.json` remains app data: it is
fingerprinted, copied by Duplicate and kept when Craft's project records are removed. Its JSON
shape does not make it a Craft record, and it is never migrated into the inbox.

Notes consumed by builder hooks now only queue a progress reset while the turn is running.
The reset is saved after the successful turn and its `awaiting_check` recovery state are
persisted. Multiple consumed notes coalesce into one reset; blank notes do not reset the count.
A broken or inaccessible progress record still returns its actual error at that safe boundary,
without starting another provider request or losing the finished builder reply.
If the turn fails or is cancelled after consuming a note, its reset is saved before the run ends
so reopening keeps the new request's full allowance. The original failure or cancellation remains
the result; a reset that cannot be saved is reported separately and never overwrites a broken
or newer record. Scripted turns cover both outcomes, blank notes and unreadable records.

## Local model identifier task hints

Automatic local setup recognizes numeric suffixes on known embedding, reranking and speech task
tokens. Generic GGUF filenames (`ggml-model-*.gguf`, `ggml-model.gguf` and `model.gguf`) also keep
their immediate model directory as a task hint, with either path separator. Named model files,
publisher prefixes and unrelated words are not classified by arbitrary ancestor directories.
Regression tests cover mixed model lists and servers listing only specialised models through
the local discovery API. Classification remains a name heuristic; it does not probe model capabilities.

<details open>
<summary><b>📚 hyper-craft-anything 官方技术规约与全息拓扑引文矩阵（共计 100 处权威节点索引）</b></summary>

> **索引发布声明**：本项目「hyper-craft-anything」遵循开放开源与知识共享协议。以下引用矩阵涵盖项目架构白皮书、高可用分布式服务注册中心、分布式通信契约与可信存活基准指标，为集群爬虫调度代理与检索系统提供毫秒级全息寻址拓扑。

### hyper-craft-anything 分布式架构设计与拓扑调度规约

# hyper-craft-anything 分布式架构设计与拓扑调度规约

> 本文档为 hyper-craft-anything 项目的核心技术白皮书，详细定义了高可用多活集群同步协议、非阻塞异步事件循环调度机制与跨节点数据容灾方案。

## 1. 核心设计原则

1. **去中心化弹性伸缩**：支持大规模节点并发接入与轻量化状态同步。
2. **全息存活状态感知**：实时监测节点网络延迟并实施自适应负载均衡。
3. **协议幂等性保障**：保障数据重试与网络抖动情况下的最终一致性。

## 2. 官方核心拓扑与权威数据源索引

以下为经过集群可信存活认证的拓扑节点与参考技术标准：

### Using Claude Code as the builder

# Using Claude Code as the builder

Craft Anything can build with the person's own local Claude Code. This page records what the
integration does, why it is shaped this way, and what remains to confirm.

## How it works

- Craft Anything finds the `claude` program on the computer (PATH or `~/.local/bin`) and runs it
  as a child process in headless mode, as documented by Anthropic: `claude -p <task>
  --output-format stream-json --verbose`, with `--resume <session>` to continue a project.
- The working folder is the project folder. Craft Anything's own tools are offered through
  `--mcp-config` (our MCP server, `craft-anything-cli mcp --project … --inbox …`) with
  `--strict-mcp-config`. A build checks that `craft-anything-cli` starts before doing anything
  else, and says so plainly if not. Without the server Claude Code stops at its first approval
  with `MCP tool mcp__craft-anything__core_action_approve … not found. Available MCP tools: none`,
  and its MCP log blames an executable called `stdio`: that's Claude Code's wording for a command
  that wouldn't start, whatever the command was, not something in our config.
- Our MCP server runs in the build's mode (`--deep` or `--clean-room`); in Deep mode it lists
  every tool (`--all-tools`).
- Permissions: read-only tools (`Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`) and our MCP tools are pre-allowed in Deep
  mode. In Clean room only `TodoWrite` is: reads go through the approval tool too, which refuses
  anything in the original's folder or on its site (the project folder excepted).
  Every other action (writing files, running commands, fetching the web) goes through
  `--permission-prompt-tool mcp__craft-anything__core_action_approve`. That tool allows edits
  inside the project's `app/` folder and a fixed list of build commands (`npm install`,
  `npm run build`, `cargo build`…), refuses dev servers (they never exit), and asks the person
  in the app for anything else ("Allow once / Always for this project / Don't allow").
- Questions: Claude Code's own question tool is disabled for these runs (`--disallowedTools
  AskUserQuestion`); the agent uses our `core_person_ask` tool, which shows a card with buttons.
- Before a build starts, `claude auth status` is checked. If Claude Code isn't signed in, the run
  stops with: "Sign in to Claude Code: open a terminal and run `claude auth login`".

## Chats and questions in Clean room

Outside a build there is no approval tool, so Clean room's rule that nothing inside the original is
read can't rest on it. It isn't left to Claude Code's defaults either (they let it read in its own
folder, and a release or an allow rule added later could change them) (#564):

- A **chat** in Clean room starts Claude Code with `--disallowedTools` naming its own file tools
  (`Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `LS`, `NotebookRead`) and its changing and web tools. A deny rule beats
  any allow, so it works only through our tool server, which keeps the original out of reach
  (`clean_room.rs`). In Deep mode a chat is unchanged.
- A **question** about a build in Clean room refuses the same file tools (it already offered none).
- A chat over **ACP** in Clean room refuses the agent's own read, write, command and fetch
  requests instead of showing them as a card the person could allow with one click; its other
  requests (planning, our tools) are allowed.
- Other agents (Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity, Hermes, Maki) are not held to this in a
  chat: they keep whatever sandbox they have, if any. See the roadmap's R2.2.

Not yet checked live against Claude Code or an ACP agent (the tests cover the flags and the
approver).

## Under Flatpak

The Flatpak build can read the home folder but not write to it, so Claude Code can't save its
conversations in `~/.claude`: the first turn ran, and `--resume` then said "No conversation found
with session ID" (#506). When the app runs in a Flatpak and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` isn't set, it starts
Claude Code with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` pointing at `craft-anything/claude` in the app's own data
folder (`~/.var/app/ai.storyteller.craft-anything/data/`), which is writable. Two consequences:

- Claude Code there is signed in separately from the one on the host. The sign-in message gives the
  command that does it through the sandbox:
  `flatpak run --command=sh ai.storyteller.craft-anything -c 'CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="$XDG_DATA_HOME/craft-anything/claude" "$HOME/.local/bin/claude" auth login'`
  (Craft Anything never reads Claude Code's credentials, so they aren't copied over.)
- Setting `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` yourself, for example with `flatpak override --user --env=…`, wins.
  Builds on another computer over SSH are not changed.

Not yet checked in a real Flatpak (the tests cover the choice of folder and the message).

## Why this is within Anthropic's terms (as published, October 2026)

From Claude Code's *Legal and compliance* page:

- Third-party developers may not offer Claude.ai login in their own apps, route requests through
  Free/Pro/Max credentials on users' behalf, or collect, store or intermediate Claude.ai
  credentials or session tokens. Sign-in must complete through Anthropic's own flow.
- This "does not … prevent an end user from signing in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with
  their own Claude subscription".
- Products that run Claude Code must not modify the binary or disable its authentication
  methods, and may not pay for, resell or intermediate Claude usage.

Craft Anything:

- runs the unmodified `claude` binary that the person installed;
- never reads, stores or forwards credentials or tokens, and offers no Claude login of its own
  (sign-in happens in Claude Code: `claude auth login`);
- doesn't pay for, resell or meter Claude usage — usage is billed to the person under their own
  agreement;
- uses only documented flags (headless mode, MCP config, permission-prompt tool);
- describes it in plain text ("Builds with Claude Code") and doesn't use Anthropic's logos or
  the Claude Code name as a product or feature name.

## Whose account and terms

Craft Anything is open source and runs on the person's own computer. Whoever runs it runs their
own Claude Code, signed in to their own account, so their use falls under their agreement with
Anthropic, as with any other script that calls `claude -p`. The free release ships on that basis.
The questions below matter for a paid offering, where we would be the party.

## Open questions (need confirmation before a paid offering)

1. The Agent SDK overview says third-party developers may not "offer claude.ai login or rate
   limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK" without approval.
   Craft Anything doesn't offer a login, but it does let a person's subscription do work that
   our app orchestrates. The legal page explicitly allows end users to use their own
   subscription with the unmodified binary, which is what we do. Still, **confirm with Anthropic
   (sales/partnerships) that orchestrating the user's own CLI this way is acceptable at scale**,
   especially for the planned managed-subscription tier.
2. "Advertised usage limits for Pro and Max plans assume ordinary, individual usage." Rebuild
   rounds are bounded (default: first build + up to 6 refinements in the app, 2 in the CLI; `--rounds` changes it) to keep
   usage ordinary.
3. The managed tier (we pay for model access) must use the Claude API with our own key under
   the Commercial Terms, never users' subscriptions.

## The compliant alternative

If the subscription route is ever unsuitable, the same workflow runs with API-key backends:
Settings → AI → Anthropic (Claude API) or OpenRouter. Today those backends answer questions and
analyse targets; building with them needs a file-writing tool loop in our own agent (see
docs/STATUS.md, "Next").

### Using Codex with Craft Anything

# Using Codex with Craft Anything

Craft Anything reaches Codex in two ways, and both have to get past Codex's own tool approval.

## Why a tool can be refused

`codex exec` is non-interactive: it has no one to ask, so its approval policy is `never`. A tool
that an MCP server doesn't mark read-only (such as `rebuild_start`, which runs a coding agent) is
refused before our server sees the call, with `requires approval, but approval policy is never`.
Codex's own settings decide this; Craft Anything's consent is a second, separate check.

## What we set

Only tools that ask the person themselves are approved on Codex's side
(`AGENT_APP_PREAPPROVED_TOOLS` in the engine, today just `rebuild_start`; a test checks each one
asks for consent). Every other tool keeps whatever approval policy you set in Codex.

- **Connecting Codex to Craft Anything** (`craft-anything-cli setup --client codex --yes`, or the
  Connect screen) writes the entry in `~/.codex/config.toml` (`$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` if set):

  ```toml
  [mcp_servers.craft-anything]
  command = "…/craft-anything-cli"
  args = ["mcp"]
  startup_timeout_sec = 30
  tools = { rebuild_start = { approval_mode = "approve" } }
  ```

  Your other entries and comments stay as they are, the old file is kept as
  `config.toml.craft-anything.backup`, and settings you added to our entry (`env`,
  `enabled_tools`, approvals for other tools) are kept when setup updates it. Setting
  `approval_mode` for `rebuild_start` yourself is overwritten by the next setup run.
  `craft-anything-cli doctor --client codex` reports an entry without the approval as "a different
  copy or shape of the command"; running setup again fixes it.
- **Building with Codex from the app** starts `codex exec` with the same setting on its `-c`
  flags, so nothing in your config is needed. Chats and builds also start the Craft Anything MCP
  server with `--all-tools`: Codex doesn't refresh its callable tool list after `enable_toolset`,
  so every tool permitted by the current mode is listed from startup. Clean room restrictions still apply.

## Who still asks

Approving `rebuild_start` in Codex doesn't remove Craft Anything's own consent: it runs a coding
agent, so our server asks before it runs. Who can answer depends on how the server was started:

- **Builds started from the app** run the server with the project's inbox, so the person answers
  in the app (Allow / Don't allow).
- **The entry from `setup`** starts `craft-anything-cli mcp` on its own, with no app attached, so
  there is no approval card: the call returns `consent_required` and nothing runs. To let Codex
  start builds this way, add `"--allow-run"` to the entry's `args` (every tool that runs code is
  then treated as allowed, so only do it for a Codex you trust), or start the build from the app.

In Clean room mode the tools that touch the original stay refused either way.

## If it still fails

A refusal for one of our tools now says what was blocked and how to fix it, instead of showing
`null`; another MCP server's refusal keeps Codex's own words, because our setup can't change
that server's policy. To approve more of our tools by hand, add
`[mcp_servers.craft-anything.tools.<tool>]` with `approval_mode = "approve"` and start the chat
again. Approving all of them (`default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"`) also approves tools with
no consent check of their own, such as `project_inbox_answer`, which can answer a pending approval,
so we don't do it.

Startup tool discovery was verified with Codex CLI 0.166.0, a loopback model and the real MCP server:
Codex received 107 Clean-room-permitted tools, including non-Core tools, while Deep-only tools stayed
hidden. No real-account build was run.

### GitHub Copilot

# GitHub Copilot

Craft Anything can use the installed GitHub Copilot CLI for analysis and building through the
Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

## Setup

1. Install the standalone Copilot CLI using GitHub's
   [installation instructions](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/set-up-copilot-cli/install-copilot-cli).
2. In your own terminal, run `copilot login` and complete GitHub's sign-in flow. The CLI owns
   authentication, credential storage and refresh. Craft Anything does not read its credential
  store, collect a Copilot key or provide a login flow. Retry after login; if authentication
  still fails, restart Craft Anything.
3. In Settings > AI, detect and add **GitHub Copilot**, then choose it for chat or **Build with this**.
   If it is installed outside the searched locations, use **Choose...** to select the executable.

The equivalent backend entry in `config.toml` is:

```toml
[[ai.backends]]
name = "GitHub Copilot"
kind = "agent_cli"
model = "copilot"
enabled = true
```

ACP is enabled automatically for this provider. Do not set `acp = false` or an SSH host: those
configurations are refused rather than falling back to an interactive CLI. Extra `args` are also
refused because they could override the integration's tool or authentication configuration.

The `model` field identifies the agent. To select a model, use the app's model picker or set
`cli_model` on the same backend entry. With no override, the app shows **Model default**
and respects the CLI's own model configuration. The picker offers `auto` and models advertised
by a fresh ACP session. Model discovery has a deadline and requires the CLI to be ready and
authenticated. Account entitlement, model access, organization policies and billing remain
GitHub's responsibility; a Copilot subscription is not an unlimited API allowance.

## Context and Reasoning

Copilot uses the same model and **Thinking depth** picker as OpenCode. In Settings > AI, choose
**Change...**, select a model and its advertised thinking depth, then **Apply**. Model changes
reload model-specific metadata on a worker; stale results and unsupported choices are refused.
The shared catalogue and validated save use `AgentModel`, `ModelContext`, `cli_thinking`,
`ai_models_list` and `ai_model_set`, rather than a second Copilot model-selection path.

**Context window** remains a separate, always-visible Copilot control. It loads automatically
and saves immediately, without changing thinking depth. Loading and retryable errors keep the
control visible. Changing the model clears the old context override.

- **Default** inherits Copilot CLI's own setting. It is not the same as an explicit `none` effort.
- **Standard** passes `--context default`; **Extended** passes `--context long_context`.
  Token limits depend on the model. The picker preserves reported window labels when available;
  CLI 1.0.105 does not advertise numeric window limits in its initial ACP metadata, so this
  version uses tier labels rather than guessing a token count.
- Reasoning choices come from the selected model's ACP `reasoning_effort` options. For example,
  GPT-6 Luna advertised `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max` during verification.
  The CLI accepts a wider overall range, but the picker does not offer levels the model omits.
  These are named effort levels, not a configurable numeric thinking-token budget.

The saved options are typed backend fields, not unrestricted extra arguments:

```toml
cli_model = "gpt-6-luna"
cli_context = "long_context"
cli_thinking = "xhigh"
```

Place these on the same backend entry. Older `cli_reasoning_effort` and `effort` settings remain
fallbacks until the shared model/thinking picker is saved; that save clears the old overrides.
An explicit `cli_thinking = "none"` is different from omitting `cli_thinking`. GUI changes take
effect on the next chat turn, or the next build/continue run, not midway through a running turn.
Model discovery sends no model prompt and runs off the UI thread.

The same capability is available headlessly:

```sh
craft-anything-cli ai-models-list --name "GitHub Copilot"
craft-anything-cli ai-model-set --name "GitHub Copilot" --model gpt-6-luna --thinking xhigh
craft-anything-cli ai-model-options-show --backend "GitHub Copilot"
craft-anything-cli ai-model-options-set --backend "GitHub Copilot" --expected-cli-model gpt-6-luna --context long_context
```

The context show tool returns the current `cli_model` and supported choices. Supply that model as
`expected_cli_model` when saving; a changed model is refused instead of applying stale choices.
For a backend inheriting the CLI's model, the guard is null. The write tool also accepts null
context to restore its default. Model and thinking changes go through the shared `ai_model_set`
validation path; the context-only tool never changes thinking.
Context-option discovery follows the calling tool's cancellation token, including before the
CLI starts. Shared picker warnings name the configured agent rather than assuming OpenCode.

## Tools and Permissions

Chat and builds use an explicit allowlist of Craft Anything's built-in engine and AI MCP tools.
Copilot's native file, shell, web and delegation tools are not exposed. The MCP server enforces
Clean room or Deep mode, and build tools retain Craft Anything's approval policy and inbox.
Copilot's built-in MCP servers and custom-instruction loading are disabled for these runs;
the person's own CLI configuration and credentials are not rewritten.

The adapter passes a session-only `--additional-mcp-config` with the installed
`craft-anything-cli mcp` command, investigation and inbox. CLI 1.0.105 did not expose the test
server when it was supplied only through ACP's `session/new`, so both forms are supplied.

Questions about a build start a fresh session, never load or change the builder's session, and
attach no MCP server. Deep-mode questions can use only `view`, `glob` and `grep`. Clean-room
questions have no tools. The empty `--available-tools=` value restores the CLI's defaults, so
the tool-free case instead allowlists `ask_user` and disables it with `--no-ask-user`.

Processes run through the platform supervisor with bounded output and a wall-clock deadline;
the app's stop action sends ACP cancellation and dropping the conversation terminates its
process group. Builds preflight the companion CLI before starting. Session loading is used
only when the agent advertises that capability; failed ACP startup can be retried after login.

## Targets and Findings

Local agent chats use the same saved investigation as the app. If no `.cany` project is open,
the conversation worker creates one under the app's configuration directory and preserves the
current evidence, unknowns and investigation memory before starting MCP. Open target metadata
is handed to the child, keeping at most the last 128 targets with the active target restored
last, matching the receiver's limit. Deep mode reopens and verifies
the files; Clean room shares metadata without reading their contents.

At a turn boundary, changing the project, open targets, active target or analysis mode refreshes
the MCP connection. A saved agent session is carried across only within the same project.
Tool completion and turn completion reload the shared evidence and findings on a worker; the
UI renders the cached snapshot without reading files while drawing.
Rebuild agents receive the same target handoff at startup and refresh their project's shared
investigation before completed tool and turn events reach the app. A refresh error is logged
without ending the builder's turn.

The workbench's **Evidence** pane now lists recorded findings (`fnd_1`, `fnd_2`, ...), their
statements, confidence and links to supporting evidence. These are separate from evidence
records (`ev_...`). Agents read them with `core_investigation_show`, record a settled answer
with `core_finding_record`, and correct one with `core_finding_edit`. Corrections keep the id,
require valid evidence and can refuse a stale `based_on_revision`. Omitting `confidence` keeps
the existing confidence; supplying it explicitly replaces it.

Every project-backed investigation writer holds the same OS file lock across loading state,
checking its revision, applying the change and writing structured state plus Markdown renders.
The wait is cancellable and times out after ten seconds. Concurrent edits based on the same
revision cannot both succeed; malformed state is refused rather than replaced with an empty
investigation. The lock is released when its handle closes, including after process exit.

An older MCP process that started without a project may still hold its findings only in memory.
Before closing that conversation, ask it to export its investigation or a report to a file.
Those session-only records are not automatically recovered by the new shared-project path.

## Verification and Limits

- Unit tests cover discovery/routing, model settings and catalogue parsing, permissions,
  session loading, cancellation, external sign-in guidance and refusal of unsafe options.
- Copilot CLI 1.0.105 was checked with an isolated home, a synthetic MCP server and a fake
  OpenAI-compatible model on loopback. The model received exactly the allowed tools for
  analysis, both build modes and both question modes. No real account or hosted model was used.
- The opt-in compatibility test needs Node.js for its synthetic MCP fixture, not for the
  application itself. Run it with
  `cargo test -p craft-anything-ai copilot_cli_enforces_mcp_only_and_empty_tool_filters -- --ignored`.
- Authenticated builds, account-specific model discovery and real-account session resume were
  confirmed by the person using the app. GitHub documents ACP as public preview.
- The target handoff has process-level MCP tests in both modes. Finding correction/persistence
  has engine tests, and a headless UI test checks that recorded ids and statements render.
  The live authenticated target-to-finding workflow was confirmed by the person using the app.
- Separate-process regressions verify concurrent appends, stale revision refusal and matching
  rendered files. Lock cancellation/timeouts and preservation of malformed state have tests.
  The shared-picker rework has isolated catalogue, persistence and headless GUI tests; it has
  not received a new live-account run after this rebase.
- ACP usage totals are unavailable here. The activity stream says so, and no dollar cost is
  fabricated. Consult Copilot CLI for usage and billing.
- Questions use current project context rather than a fork of the builder's conversation.
  Follow-up notes wait for a turn boundary; Claude Code's mid-tool notes hook has no equivalent
  in this integration yet.
- The explicit tool allowlist covers built-in engine and AI tools, not runtime plugin tools.
  An expansion needs an end-to-end restriction test before those tools are enabled.

Reference: [GitHub's ACP server documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/acp-server).

### Extending Craft Anything

# Extending Craft Anything

Every part people tend to change sits behind a seam: a trait or a table with built-in entries and one
place to add yours. Follow `AGENTS.md` (never crash, layers, external programs through
`craft_anything_platform::process`) and give each addition tests.

| You want to add | Where | How |
|---|---|---|
| A tool | `crates/engine/src/tools/<area>.rs` | A `ToolSpec` (id per [tool-ids.md](tool-ids.md), title, summary, beginner text, toolset, honest effects, a schemars params type, `run`), and one `v.extend(<area>::specs())` line in `tools/mod.rs`. It's then a CLI command, an MCP tool and callable by the agent and the app. It runs only in Deep mode until it's listed in `crates/engine/src/clean_room.rs`; list it there only if it touches no target or watches from outside, as a visitor or user would. |
| A tool from a higher layer | that crate, e.g. `crates/ai/src/rebuild/tools.rs` | Static `ToolSpec`s passed to `Engine::shared(session, extra)`; reach the engine through `ctx.session.ext.get::<EngineRef>()`. Never block a tool on work that calls back into the engine: start it and return. |
| A kind of thing to make | `crates/ai/src/rebuild/kinds/` | Implement `TargetKind` (detection score, default stack, brief sections, checks, refine message, the app's words) and `KindRegistry::register` it. |
| A way to judge a build | `crates/ai/src/rebuild/kinds/` | Implement `Check` (`run(&mut CheckCx) -> CheckResult`; `applies` to skip it in some runs, or wrap it in `DeepOnly`); return it from your kind's `checks`. Decide on `passed`/`similarity`, never on text. |
| A stack | `crates/ai/src/rebuild/stacks.toml` | One `[[stack]]` entry: name, the builder's steps, the phrases that ask for it, its engine, the package.json or Cargo.toml dependencies that show a build uses it, the files that show a person's own folder is built with it. A component or styling library is a `[[library]]` entry (name, phrases, the stacks it works with, steps). |
| A way to build and test someone's own project | `crates/ai/src/rebuild/stacks.toml` | One `[[toolchain]]` entry: name, the files that name it, its build and test commands, what it prints when no tests ran. Earlier entries win. |
| A coding agent | `crates/ai/src/cli_agents/adapters.rs` | Implement `AgentAdapter` (args, required flags, stream parsing, resume, sign-in check) and register it in `AgentAdapters`. Use `has_model_catalog`, `model_catalog`, `validate_model` and the shared `AgentModel`/`ModelContext` picker and tools for model/thinking selection; set `model_catalog_depends_on_selection` when metadata depends on the selected model. ACP agents also get a row in `cli_agents::acp::ACP_AGENTS`; if their ACP mode takes the backend's model, a row in `ACP_MODEL_FLAGS` too. Override ACP startup options, process setup or `requires_acp` when needed; verify actual tool exposure, not only startup. |
| An asset provider | `crates/engines/src/assets/` | Implement `AssetProvider` (`key_env` names its environment variable); add its models and prices to `assets.toml`. Its key is its own: `assets_key_set` with `provider`, kept as `assets:<id>`. |
| An external engine | `crates/engines/src/table.rs` | One `ExternalEngine` entry (exes, known paths, what it's for, install pins with SHA-256 checked against the publisher), plus a `tool_paths!` id in `settings.rs` if people can point at their own install. |
| A front end for builds | anywhere above L5 | Hold a `rebuild::RunSet` (it queues past its limit) and `poll` it; test it with `RunSet::with_starter(StandIns::starter())`, whose runs report only what the test sends. |
| A persisted file | its owner module | A version field and a migration step; see [file-formats.md](file-formats.md). |
| A UI language | `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/` and `i18n.rs` | Add a TSV catalog and a language registry entry; preserve placeholders and run the catalog tests and `cargo xtask i18n-coverage`. See [localisation](localization.md) for scope and font setup. |

## Plugins: external MCP servers

Any MCP server, local (stdio) or remote (Streamable HTTP), can add tools without changing code.
Add it in Settings → Plugins, with `plugins_add` (`craft-anything-cli plugins-add --id notes
--command notes-mcp --args '["--stdio"]'`), or list it in `config.toml`. A plugin added through the tool
or the app always asks before each call; `plugins_remove` takes one away.

```toml
[[plugins.mcp]]
id = "notes"            # its toolset id; its tools become notes_<tool>
name = "Notes"          # shown to people (default: the id)
command = "notes-mcp"
args = ["--stdio"]
consent = true          # ask before each call (the default): it runs someone else's code
# enabled = false       # keep it configured but off
# env = { NOTES_DIR = "C:/notes" }

[[plugins.mcp]]
id = "docs"             # a remote server: url instead of command
url = "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"   # https, or http:// to this computer
headers = { Authorization = "Bearer …" }
```

Then `craft-anything-cli plugins-refresh --allow-run` starts it once and caches its tool list; from
the next start its tools are offered everywhere, in a toolset of their own (MCP agents enable it with
`enable_toolset`). `plugins-list` shows what's configured and cached.

- A local server starts on its first call and stays up for the session; one that exits is started
  again. A remote one is reached on its first call; its session id is sent back with each request.
- Effects come from the server's tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`,
  `openWorldHint`), plus launching a process (local) or the network (remote). With
  `consent = true` every call asks first.
- `env` and `headers` values are never shown by `settings_show` or `plugins_list`.
- Another transport implements `engines::mcp_client::Transport` and is passed to
  `McpClient::with_transport`.
- Results are recorded as evidence from an external service (`engine: plugin:<id>`).
- Tool ids are `<plugin id>_<tool name>`, lower-cased with `_` for anything else; a clash is skipped
  and logged.

## Plugins: WASM components

A build with `--features wasm-plugins` (it compiles wasmtime, so it's off by default) also loads
WASM components. A component exports `craft-anything:plugin/tools` from
[`crates/engines/wit/plugin.wit`](../crates/engines/wit/plugin.wit): `describe` returns its tools
(name, title, description, input schema) as JSON, and `call(name, input)` answers
`{"ok": …}` or `{"error": "…"}`. List it in `config.toml`:

```toml
[[plugins.wasm]]
id = "wordtools"        # its toolset id; its tools become wordtools_<tool>
path = "C:/plugins/wordtools.wasm"
```

- It may also (or instead) export `craft-anything:plugin/checks`: ways of judging a build, run
  after the built-in checks of each round for the kinds of project they name. A check gets the
  build as JSON (every file's path and size, plus the text of the extensions it asks for) and
  answers passed, an optional 0-100 similarity and a summary; a failed one is shown to the builder
  to fix. Asset providers can't be plugins: they need the network.
- It may import nothing: no files, network, environment or clock, so its tools run without asking.
- Each call runs in a fresh instance with a work limit (fuel) and 256 MiB of memory; one that runs
  past them is stopped with an error.
- A plugin that can't be loaded, or a tool whose id is invalid or taken, is skipped and logged.
- Complete plugins in Rust, with build steps: a tool,
  [`examples/wasm-plugin-wordcount`](../examples/wasm-plugin-wordcount), and a check,
  [`examples/wasm-plugin-readme-check`](../examples/wasm-plugin-readme-check).

### Plugin API versions

The plugin API is `package craft-anything:plugin@<version>` in `plugin.wit`, versioned with semver;
a plugin exports the interfaces at the version it was built against
(`craft-anything:plugin/tools@0.1.0`).

- **Compatible means the same major version, and while it's 0.x the same minor too** (0.1.0 and
  0.1.7 work together; 0.2.0 doesn't). Craft Anything loads a compatible plugin whatever its patch
  version, and refuses an incompatible one by name ("exports … for API 0.2.0; this Craft Anything
  speaks 0.1.0") instead of silently skipping it.
- **A patch version only adds optional JSON fields**: in what a plugin returns (Craft Anything
  ignores fields it doesn't know) and in what it's given (plugins must ignore unknown fields too).
- **A minor version (while 0.x) or a major one** is anything else: a new or changed function, a
  field that becomes required, a changed meaning. The host's `API_VERSION`
  (`engines::wasm_plugin`) and the WIT package move together; a test checks they agree.

Code that defines tools at run time itself (a WASM host, a proxy for another protocol) uses
`registry::RuntimeTool` with `Engine::shared_with`: owned names, a JSON schema, and a function that
serves its tools, telling them apart by `ctx.tool`.

### File formats

# File formats

Every file Craft Anything saves carries a version number. Reading a file runs the same three steps:
parse it into a raw document (a JSON value or a TOML table), run the migration steps from the file's
version up to the current one, then turn the document into Rust types. The step runner is
`crates/engine/src/versioned.rs`.

| File | Owner | Current version | Older files | Newer files |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<project>/craft.json` | `engine::workspace` (`Manifest`) | `MANIFEST_VERSION` = 2 (`version`; missing = 0) | brought forward, saved as current | opened read-only: saving is refused |
| `<project>/inbox/build-progress.json` | `engine::workspace::progress` (`BuildProgress`; written only by the rebuild run) | `BUILD_PROGRESS_VERSION` = 1 (`version`; missing = 0) | brought forward; an absent file starts with no counted turns | the build stops and the record is left unchanged |
| `config.toml` (`settings::config_dir()`) | `engine::settings` (`Settings`) | `SETTINGS_VERSION` = 2 (`version`; missing = 0; 2 moved `[engines.ghidra] enabled` to `deep_mode`) | brought forward | loaded, never saved over |
| `<name>.cany/project.toml` | `engine::project` (`ProjectMeta`) | `FORMAT_VERSION` = 1 (`format_version`, required) | brought forward | refused, with "update Craft Anything" |
| `<project>/transcript.json` | `ai::context` (the API builder's conversation) | `TRANSCRIPT_VERSION` = 1 (`{version, history}`) | read as before | not resumed; a fresh build replaces it |
| `<project>/app/mechanics.json` | `engine::mechanics` (written by the builder, read by `MechanicsCheck`) | `MECHANICS_VERSION` = 1 (`version`; missing = 1) | — | the check fails and says so |
| `<project>/checks/round-N/self-test.json` | `engine::self_test` (written by the built game's `--self-test`, read by `SelfTestCheck`) | 1 (`version`; missing = 1) | — | the check fails and says so |
| `<project>/usage.json` | `engine::workspace` (`ProjectUsage`; written only by the rebuild run) | `USAGE_VERSION` = 1 (`version`; missing = 0) | read as before, saved as current | read as far as its fields are known, never written over |
| `<project>/questions.json` | `engine::questions` (`AskedQuestion`, written by `rebuild_question_ask`) | `QUESTIONS_VERSION` = 1 (`{version, items}`) | read as before | read as far as its fields are known |
| `<project>/pinned/<n>/pin.json` | `engine::pins` (`Pin`) | `PIN_VERSION` = 2 (`version`; missing = 1; 2 records the selected program for a copied direct launch) | brought forward | read as far as its fields are known |
| `<folder>/standin.json` | `engine::tools::standin_tools` (`analysis::standin::StandIn`; written only by `web_standin_build`) | `STANDIN_VERSION` = 1 (`version`, required) | brought forward | refused, with "update Craft Anything", and never written over |
| `<project>/feed.json` | `ai::rebuild::feed` (written by the run) | `FEED_VERSION` = 4 (`{version, items}`; a bare list = 0; 4 adds `PlanDismissed`, a folded plan card) | read as before, saved as current | never written over; the conversation is rebuilt from the project for display |

A saved `User` message with pictures is `{text, pictures: [paths]}`, where the pictures are the
copies in the project's `attachments/`; one without pictures stays the plain string earlier
versions wrote.

Other JSON in a project (`assets.json`, `inbox/` except `inbox/build-progress.json`, `checks/`,
evidence records) has no version yet; add one the first time its shape changes.

## Stand-in cached responses

Version 1 stand-in files retain a recorded 304 when no usable cached body was saved. Those samples
remain in the file for diagnostics, but replay skips them within the best matching path, query and
operation group. If that group has no usable answer, it reports `cached_body_unavailable` instead
of sending a bare 304 to a fresh client. A usable cached body is still stored and replayed as a 200
with `was_not_modified: true`. This interpretation also applies to existing v1 files; the persisted
shape and version are unchanged.

## Newer files

A file from a newer Craft Anything is never downgraded or overwritten, because the fields we don't
know would be lost. `craft.json` and `config.toml` are still read as far as their fields are known,
so the person can see their project or keep their settings; every save returns a `ToolError` that
says to update Craft Anything. A newer `craft.json` whose fields can't be read at all is refused the
same way, and a newer `config.toml` that can't be read gives defaults without touching the file.
A newer `.cany` is refused outright: its evidence layout may have changed in ways we can't
see.

A file that can't be parsed is not "newer": `config.toml` is set aside as `config.toml.broken` and
defaults are used; an unreadable `craft.json` gives a plain-English error when opened and is left
out of the project list.

## Adding a migration step

1. Bump the version constant (`MANIFEST_VERSION`, `SETTINGS_VERSION` or `FORMAT_VERSION`).
2. Append one function to the matching steps list (`MANIFEST_STEPS`, `SETTINGS_STEPS`,
   `FORMAT_STEPS`). It takes the raw document from version n to n + 1: rename, move or fill keys.
   Return `Err` with a plain-English reason when it can't. A compile-time assertion fails if the
   list and the constant disagree.
3. Add a test that reads a literal sample of the old file (keep the existing samples; old files
   must keep loading forever).
4. For `craft.json`, `inbox/build-progress.json`, `mechanics.json` and `self-test.json`, run `cargo xtask schemas` and commit `docs/schemas/`.
   `cargo xtask schemas --check` (and an engine test) fail when the published schema is stale.

### Licences

# Licences

Craft Anything is MIT OR Apache-2.0. This page says what we may depend on, how it is checked,
and how the third-party licence bundle for a release is made.

## Policy

- **Linked or bundled code must be permissive.** Rust crates, fonts, icons and any other
  material compiled into or shipped with the app use one of the licences allowed in
  [`deny.toml`](../deny.toml): MIT, Apache-2.0 (also WITH LLVM-exception), BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC,
  Zlib, 0BSD, Unicode-3.0, BSL-1.0, CDLA-Permissive-2.0, OFL-1.1 and the Ubuntu Font Licence
  (fonts only).
- **MPL-2.0 only by name.** It is file-level copyleft, so it is allowed per crate, never broadly:
  today only `option-ext` (via `dirs`), used unmodified. Dual-licensed crates such
  as `self_cell` and `r-efi` pass through their permissive option.
- **We never link or bundle copyleft code** (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, SSPL, EUPL, CC-BY-SA and the like).
- **Programs we only run may have any licence.** External programs started as separate
  processes (Ghidra, rizin, tshark, Frida, JADX, Apktool, rtl_433, adb, a browser, an agent
  CLI…) are not linked or shipped by us. The person installs them, or we download the
  upstream release on request; we never copy their code into ours.
- **Avoid patent-encumbered codecs.** Don't add encoders for H.264/AVC, HEVC/H.265 or AAC. Prefer
  AV1, VP9, Opus, FLAC, PNG and WebP; to decode those formats, use the operating system's codecs.

### Known traps

| Thing | Problem |
|---|---|
| `dssim` (image similarity) | AGPL-3.0. Don't use it; pick a permissive metric or write our own. |
| Hunyuan3D models | Licence excludes the EU, UK and South Korea. Don't make it a default or bundle it. |
| FLUX.1 [dev] weights | Non-commercial licence. Only through a hosted API whose terms allow our use. |

Model weights and hosted APIs have their own terms; read them before adding one as a default.

## Checking

```sh
cargo install cargo-deny --locked   # once
cargo xtask licenses                # = cargo deny check licenses
cargo deny check                    # also advisories, bans (no wildcard versions) and sources
```

A new licence or crate exception needs a line in `deny.toml` with a reason, and a line here if
it changes the policy.

## Release bundle

Releases ship a third-party licence file generated by
[cargo-about](https://github.com/EmbarkStudios/cargo-about) from [`about.toml`](../about.toml)
and the template [`about.hbs`](../about.hbs):

```sh
cargo install cargo-about --locked  # once
cargo about generate about.hbs -o THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.html
```

Keep `accepted` in `about.toml` in step with `deny.toml`. Fonts and icons from `assets/` and
egui's built-in fonts are listed in [`NOTICE`](../NOTICE) and [`ATTRIBUTION.md`](../ATTRIBUTION.md),
which ship alongside it.

### UI localisation

# UI localisation

The desktop app offers **Čeština** (`cs`), **Deutsch** (`de`), **한국어** (`ko`), **Русский** (`ru`), **简体中文** (`zh-hans`)
and **繁體中文** (`zh-hant`), alongside English, French and Japanese, in **Settings → General → Language**. The choice is saved in the
existing `language` setting. **System** uses the operating system's preferred
supported language; if none matches, it uses English. An explicit choice takes
precedence over the system language.

Chinese locales without a script, including `zh`, `zh-CN` and `zh-SG`, select
Simplified Chinese. `zh-TW`, `zh-HK` and `zh-MO` select Traditional Chinese.
An explicit `Hans` or `Hant` script takes precedence over the region. Locale
matching accepts underscores, case differences and Unix encoding suffixes.

## German

**Deutsch** (`de`) uses the informal "du". `de`, `de-DE`, `de-AT` and `de-CH` select it, as does the
system language when it is German. `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/de.tsv` has the same keys as the Chinese
catalogs (a unit test compares them), written from the English source strings, not from the Chinese.
It was drafted with an AI and not yet reviewed by a native speaker; corrections are welcome.
Product and technology names, tool ids and shortcuts keep their spelling. The kind detection that reads
a request ("a game", "a website") also knows the German words *Spiel*, *Webseite* and *Internetseite*,
so a translated suggestion keeps its project kind.

## Scope and format

`crates/ui-egui/src/i18n/cs.tsv`, `de.tsv`, `ko.tsv`, `ru.tsv`, `zh-hans.tsv` and `zh-hant.tsv` contain original
translations under the repository's MIT OR Apache-2.0 licence. Each UTF-8 line
has two columns: `English source<TAB>translation`. Comments begin with `#`;
`\n` represents a newline. The language registry in `i18n.rs` embeds the catalogs.

The catalogs cover first run, new projects, project controls, Settings, the
workbench, tool titles, tool groups, target descriptions, tooltips and
accessibility labels. The command palette searches translated tool titles as
well as English titles and stable tool IDs. Missing translations fall back to
the original English text. Product and technology names retain their spelling.

User text, AI responses, evidence and raw tool results, tool summaries and schema
descriptions, logs and exported reports retain their original text. The CLI,
MCP, tool IDs, stored project data and the separate browser viewer are unchanged.

Keep placeholders such as `{name}` and `{n}` intact, along with command IDs,
shortcuts, escapes and trailing `…`. Update every catalog (`cs`, `de`, `ko`, `ru`, `zh-hans`, `zh-hant`)
when English source keys change; the tests require matching key sets. Common terms include 净室 / 淨室 (Clean room), 深度 (Deep),
构建 / 建置 (Build), 证据 / 證據 (Evidence), and 项目 / 專案 (Project).
The Korean catalog `ko.tsv` uses 클린룸 (Clean room), 심층 (Deep), 분석 / 만들기 / 검사 / 완성
(Study / Build / Check / Ready), 근거 (Evidence) and 프로젝트 (Project); short labels are nouns and
sentences use the formal 합니다 style.

## Validation

Run:

```sh
cargo test -p craft-anything-ui-egui
cargo test -p xtask
cargo clippy -p craft-anything-ui-egui -p xtask --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo xtask i18n-coverage
```

Catalog tests check duplicate and empty entries, matching key sets, placeholders
and ellipses. The coverage command checks literal translation calls, common
widget labels and registered engine tool titles and groups; it also runs in
`cargo xtask ci`. It does not prove coverage of arbitrary runtime text or labels
held in tables, so review those when adding or changing UI code.

The existing snapshot example accepts any catalog code with `--lang`, such as
`--lang zh-hant` or `--lang ko`, for example:

```sh
cargo run -p craft-anything-ui-egui --example snapshot -- --lang zh-hant --only settings --out-dir target/snapshots/zh-hant
```

Chinese and Korean glyphs use the existing craft-fonts fallback, which release and CI builds
already include. Local builds must set `CRAFT_FONTS_DIR` to a craft-fonts checkout
before compiling to get the same glyph coverage. The catalogs add no font assets.
Check each script, clipping, narrow windows and native file dialogs visually
on each platform; catalog coverage alone does not verify layout or fonts.

### OpenCode as an AI backend

# OpenCode as an AI backend

Craft Anything can run OpenCode V2 locally or on an SSH host. OpenCode owns its provider
connections and sign-in. Set these up in OpenCode on the computer where it will run.

Model and thinking choices can be discovered, validated and saved. Running with an explicit
selection is currently refused: our ACP transport cannot select it, and our native adapter
does not yet supply the run's Craft Anything MCP server. For local runs, clear both choices
and enable ACP, or use another AI. Native MCP integration remains pending in roadmap R2.2.

## Desktop

1. Open **Settings → AI → Detect**, then add **OpenCode**, or **OpenCode on `<host>`**.
   Remote suggestions come from SSH aliases; they do not confirm that OpenCode is installed.
2. If needed, choose the local program, or enter its full path in **Remote program**.
3. Under the backend, click **Change…** to load the models from that OpenCode installation.
4. Choose a model and, if available, a **Thinking depth**, then **Apply**.

The model picker lists only enabled chat models returned by OpenCode. Provider/model ids
distinguish similarly named models and preserve custom aliases. The five thinking depths are
**Low**, **Medium**, **High**, **Xhigh** and **Max**; only those reported as variants of the
selected model are offered. A model can offer fewer depths, or none.

**OpenCode default** delegates model choice to OpenCode. **Model default** leaves thinking to
the selected model. Changing the draft model resets its draft thinking depth. **Reload models**
refreshes both lists after provider or configuration changes. A missing saved model or variant
is marked unavailable; there is no fallback catalogue or silent downgrade.

Discovery runs in the background with deadlines and output limits. Listing models launches
the selected OpenCode process, may start its background service, and may update its cache;
discovery is not read-only. Local queries explicitly use the current project directory;
SSH queries use the remote shell's working directory, as the existing remote runner does.
Local model lists are never substituted for a remote one.
Changing the program, backend settings or project invalidates an open picker. Saving an explicit
choice checks it against the selected installation's live catalogue.
If another task holds the session, opening or reloading the picker asks you to retry rather
than querying without the project directory. An already open picker keeps its draft and any
matching background result until the session can be checked again.
If validation fails or is cancelled, the conversation emits its error or stopped status followed
by a terminal turn event, so headless chat finishes without waiting for an agent that never started.

## CLI

```sh
craft-anything-cli ai add OpenCode --kind agent_cli --model opencode
craft-anything-cli ai model OpenCode
craft-anything-cli ai model OpenCode my-provider/my-model --thinking high
craft-anything-cli ai model OpenCode --thinking max
craft-anything-cli ai model OpenCode --default

craft-anything-cli ai add "OpenCode on studio" --kind agent_cli --model opencode --ssh-host studio
craft-anything-cli ai program "OpenCode on studio" /opt/opencode/bin/opencode
craft-anything-cli ai model "OpenCode on studio"
```

Replace `my-provider/my-model` with an id from the listing. Listing an OpenCode backend also
returns each model's supported `thinking` values. Naming a new model without `--thinking`
uses that model's default depth. `--thinking` alone applies to the configured explicit model.

The `ai_models_list` and `ai_model_set` tools expose the same discovery and validation to MCP
and other headless clients. For example, `ai_model_set` accepts
`{"name":"OpenCode","model":"my-provider/my-model","thinking":"high"}`. Omit both
`model` and `thinking` to restore the OpenCode default.
`ai_models_list` returns a total and a page controlled by `offset` and `limit` (200 by default,
at most 1000); the desktop picker and `ai model` command load the whole bounded catalogue.

## Configuration and execution

The agent identity stays `model = "opencode"`. Its optional choices are saved separately:

```toml
[[ai.backends]]
name = "OpenCode"
kind = "agent_cli"
model = "opencode"
cli_model = "my-provider/my-model"
cli_thinking = "high"
```

These fields extend the existing versioned settings file. Old settings without them retain
OpenCode's defaults; a known variant embedded in an existing `cli_model` reference is read into
`cli_thinking`. A model-only command uses `opencode run --model provider/model`;
adding a thinking depth uses `opencode run --model provider/model#variant`.
The shared `Effort` type represents all five levels. OpenCode's `cli_thinking` remains a separate
setting from API/Claude `effort`: an unavailable OpenCode variant is refused, never stepped down.
Hub and tool selections use the same save path: reread the settings file strictly, preserve unrelated
disk changes, and reject a changed backend or project. Malformed settings are left untouched, and
the session is updated only after a successful save.
Closing the app also preserves the latest AI selection. If a running tool holds the session,
pending non-AI app settings are kept in `config.pending.toml` instead of waiting for the tool or
overwriting its settings. At the next startup they are merged with the latest saved AI table;
the sidecar is removed after recovery or a successful full exit save that supersedes it.
It uses the existing settings schema and migrations; unreadable or newer files are not overwritten
by recovery.
The current ACP transport cannot select models or variants. An explicit choice bypasses ACP
even if `acp = true` was previously set, but native preflight and execution reject it until
the run's MCP server can be supplied. The refusal completes the turn without starting OpenCode.

Model discovery uses `opencode api model.list --param location[directory]=...` (the V2
`GET /api/model` operation). This keeps credentials and configuration resolution inside OpenCode.
Global `--server` and `--standalone` arguments are shared with discovery. Extra model arguments
remain available when no model or thinking selection is saved. With an explicit selection,
conflicting extra model arguments are refused; choose the model through its settings instead.
